periods.analysis: We opened this sequence at 93.4%, which is solidly green against the >=90% target and gives Council a clean baseline for the City Strategic Plan service story. Because this is the first quarter in the series, there is no priorValue or delta to report, so I am treating 93.4% as our operating reference point. The Harborview Connect queue was helped by disciplined daily triage from the Resident Services desk, especially on parks lighting, missed-cart, and coastal access maintenance requests along Routes 4 and Data quality also looked strong after departments adopted the shared closure codes, which reduces the usual end-of-quarter cleanup scramble.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the daily 8:30 a.m. Harborview Connect triage huddle and keep the shared closure-code guide attached to every department queue. Before the next reporting cycle closes, have Public Works and Parks audit 25 completed tickets each for response-date accuracy so the green result stays defensible. Use 93.4% as the baseline in the Council packet and call out the departments that are already meeting the rhythm.

periods.analysis: Q4 came in at 92.9%, a -0.5 point movement from 93.4%, and still comfortably green. The small dip is not alarming, but it matches what we saw operationally during the December king-tide cleanup and the holiday staffing pattern at the Permit Center front counter. Harborview Connect ticket aging was concentrated in facilities work orders for Pier Hall and two traffic-signal timing requests on Seabreeze Avenue, not in broad citywide slippage. The important thing is that departments kept the on-time reporting cycle intact even with seasonal volume and leave schedules.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green performance by keeping the pre-holiday staffing template, but add a named backup approver for Facilities and Transportation closures in weeks with fewer than four business days. Ask Resident Services to flag king-tide-related requests with a seasonal code so we can separate true performance drift from weather-driven volume. For the Council update, frame the -0.5 change as watchful but well-managed, with no change to the green status.

periods.analysis: Q1 improved to 93.7%, a +0.8 point movement from 92.9%, putting us back above the Q3 baseline and still green. This rebound reflects the January queue reset, when supervisors cleared 142 aged but completed Harborview Connect items that were waiting only on documentation. The strongest contributors were Code Compliance nuisance-abatement closures and Public Works pothole tickets on the Bayfront, Larch, and Vista routes after the wet-weather patching crew moved to a two-day sweep. The story for Council is simple: the system caught a seasonal dip, corrected it, and preserved resident-facing reliability.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the January queue-reset practice as a standing first-week-of-quarter task owned by each department scorecard liaison. Extend the two-day pothole sweep routing model to sidewalk trip-hazard tickets, starting with the Bayfront and Marina districts where resident submissions are highest. Keep publishing the aged-ticket list every Friday at noon so department directors have time to clean it up before the reporting deadline.

periods.analysis: Q2 rose to 95%, a +1.3 point movement from 93.7%, giving us the best result in this sequence so far and a strong green signal. The service request team benefited from the spring Harborview Connect workflow refresh, including auto-routing tree-trim requests to Urban Forestry Crew UF-2 and short-term rental complaints to the correct Code Compliance cohort. Permit counter inquiries also closed faster after the Development Services vendor turned on the Accela-to-Connect status feed in May. This is the kind of operational polish that makes departments look good because the resident experience and the reporting evidence line up.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the auto-routing rules that drove the 95% result and require departments to review exception queues by 3 p.m. each Wednesday. Extend the Accela-to-Connect feed dashboard to include building inspection reschedule requests before summer construction volume peaks. Capture the workflow refresh as a one-page playbook so the improvement survives staff vacations and onboarding.

periods.analysis: Q3 eased to 92.6%, a -2.4 point movement from 95%, but it remains green and above the >=90% target. The decline is the first meaningful softening in the arc, and it tracks with summer tourism volume, beach-parking complaints, and bulky-item pickup requests around Harbor Days. We also had a temporary backlog in the Marina District graffiti queue after vendor Coastal CleanWorks changed its Tuesday route to Thursday, which added avoidable aging to a small number of tickets. I would not overstate the risk, but I would mark this as a friendly nudge moment: green, yes, but with a clear watch-item on seasonal surge planning.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the summer surge dashboard live through September rather than retiring it after Harbor Days. Direct Public Works to renegotiate the Coastal CleanWorks graffiti route back to a Tuesday or Wednesday service window for the Marina District. For next Q3 planning, pre-stage a seasonal Resident Services cohort for beach-parking and bulky-item categories so high-volume tickets do not age in the general queue.

periods.analysis: Q4 moved to 91.5%, a -1.1 point change from 92.6%, still green but now closer to the target line than we have been. The continued softening reflects year-end factors: holiday closures, a spike in storm-drain inlet reports after the November atmospheric river, and a slower handoff between Field Operations and the contractor documenting catch basin work orders SD-118 through SD-146. The good news is that the departments kept the result above 90% while also protecting data integrity, which I would rather defend than a prettier number built on rushed closures. This quarter sets up a practical recovery agenda instead of a crisis narrative.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the disciplined closure standards and do not encourage departments to close storm-drain tickets until the resident-facing work is actually complete. Add a 48-hour documentation requirement for contractor-supported storm-drain work orders, with Field Operations confirming SD-series assets every Monday and Thursday. Before the Q1 reporting deadline, have each department identify its top two aging categories so the rebound work is targeted, not generic.

periods.analysis: Q1 rebounded to 93.5%, a +2 point movement from 91.5%, which is exactly the kind of recovery we wanted to see while staying green. The improvement came from the January aging-category review and the new Monday/Thursday documentation cadence for storm-drain and facilities tickets. Resident Services also piloted a 10-ticket same-day callback cohort for unresolved Harborview Connect items over seven days old, and that helped close the loop on cases that were technically waiting on resident confirmation. The chronological story is now stronger: we absorbed two softer quarters, fixed the handoffs, and moved back toward our normal performance band.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Monday/Thursday documentation cadence through the end of the rainy season and keep it visible on the department director dashboard. Extend the same-day callback cohort from 10 tickets to 20 tickets per week, prioritizing cases older than seven days in Public Works, Code Compliance, and Parks. Use the +2 movement in the Council narrative to show that the watch-items produced action, not just commentary.

periods.analysis: Q2 improved again to 94%, a +0.5 point movement from 93.5%, keeping the measure green and confirming that Q1 was not a one-quarter bounce. The strongest operational detail is consistency: Harborview Connect queues were reviewed before every month-end close, and the Permit Center's expanded Accela status feed reduced duplicate resident inquiries during the spring construction season. Parks also used its Beach Ready checklist to close restroom, signage, and access-path requests before Memorial Day weekend rather than carrying them into summer. We are not back to the 95% high-water mark from 2025-Q2, but we are in a healthy, reliable band with better controls than we had a year ago.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the month-end queue review and make it a required ClearPoint evidence attachment for each department's quarterly update. Extend the Beach Ready checklist model to winter storm readiness, with asset IDs for priority drains, pump stations, and coastal access points loaded before October. Set a management aim of returning to 95% without loosening closure standards, and report the top three aging categories to directors two weeks before each quarter closes.

periods.analysis: The resolution rate improved from 91.2% to 91.8%, remaining above the 90% target. This is a favorable service outcome, not evidence that every strategic project is on schedule.
periods.recommendations: Keep the month-end queue review and flag aging requests separately from closed requests.
